title: Phase-sensitive avalanche quantum sensing of sub-shot-noise fields
abstract: Avalanche-based detection of small perturbations is commonplace in precision measurement devices from Geiger counters to single-photon avalanche detectors. Here, we expand this principle to sensing of light waves below the quantum shot noise limit, demonstrating numerically how atomic clouds trapped in photonic cavities can exhibit non-perturbative sensitivity to changes in the cavity field when the cavity mode is tuned to a parity-prohibited transition. We find that, when pumped by a continuous-wave laser, the atomic cloud creates emissions which amplify the initially sub-shot-noise fluctuation by two orders of magnitude. Crucially, this amplification is broadly tunable with respect to frequency and independent of atomic energy structure. Even more strikingly, our amplification mechanism preserves the phase imparted on the atoms by the original ultra-weak light wave, marking a qualitative improvement over conventional protocols. Our finding has implications for both quantum state characterization and detection of weak classical signals.
summary: This paper proposes using atomic ensembles in photonic cavities as quantum avalanche detectors to sense light fields below the standard quantum shot noise limit. By tuning the cavity resonance, the system achieves a massive, tunable amplification of weak light fluctuations. Crucially, this mechanism preserves the phase information of the original weak signal, offering an improvement over existing quantum sensing protocols.
main_problem: To develop a quantum sensing technique that detects sub-shot-noise fluctuations in light fields by leveraging atomic ensembles trapped in photonic cavities.
main_result: The atomic cloud acts as a quantum avalanche detector, amplifying initial sub-shot-noise fluctuations by two orders of magnitude while preserving the phase of the weak input light.
method: The study employs the non-perturbative Hierarchy of Pure States (HOPS) method to model the complex, continuously driven quantum dynamics.
model_or_system: The system consists of atomic clouds coupled to photonic cavities, described by Hamiltonians involving dipole operators and cavity field operators. The process is designed to utilize second-harmonic emission triggered by vacuum fluctuations.
key_observables: The evolution of the Husimi function $Q(\alpha)$ and the time-dependent average output field $\langle \hat{F} angle$ are key diagnostics.
important_parameters: The cavity tuning to the second harmonic ($2\omega$) is crucial, and the sensitivity is measured relative to the quantum shot noise limit.
main_assumptions: The approach is non-perturbative, and the simulation relies on the HOPS method due to the continuously driven nature of the system.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the basic setup, the evolution of the Husimi function under perturbation, and the time evolution of the output field amplitude.
paper_structure: The paper builds the theoretical framework by defining the Hamiltonian, applying the HOPS method to model the non-Markovian dynamics, and then demonstrating the amplification and phase preservation through numerical simulation of the output observables.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum measurement limitations by proposing a novel, high-gain, phase-sensitive detection mechanism using cavity QED systems, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (color online) Basic design of our setup. The classical radiation (red), resonant in our case with the atomic tran- sitions, drives ultrafast currents in all atoms independently. This causes them to emit frequency-converted photons (blue) entangled with the emitters. The electromagnetic radiation confinement in a medium causes these photons (blue beams with white lines) to linger, allowing them to either be ab- sorbed by the same or another atom, or leave the confining medium. In the latter case, they can be observed by a classi- cal detector positioned outside (right).
FIG. 2. Vacuum Husimi function overlaid with the coherent displacement amplitudes αp used in this work as perturba- tions.

FIG. 3. Evolution of the 3rd cavity mode’s Husimi function depending on the perturbation’s phase (left to right) and evo- lution time (top to bottom). For comparison, the rightmost column shows the time-evolving Husimi function for the un- perturbed system.

FIG. 4. Time-dependent output field shapes plotted for vary- ing perturbing field phase. The phases plotted are: π/2 (blue), π (yellow), 3π/2 (green), 2π (magenta). The thin lines indicate the initially introduced fluctuation.
